events.what: Every visa applicant is to be checked against one shared system of law-enforcement and intelligence records.
events.note: Dots show FY2011, the earliest year on this map.
events.title: Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry Reform Act
events.src: Sec. 202(a)(2)–(3), enrolled text of H.R. 3525 (Pub. L. 107–173) · congress.gov
events.quote: Upon the date of commencement of implementation of the plan required by section 201(c), the President shall develop and implement an interoperable electronic data system to provide current and immediate access to information in databases of Federal law enforcement agencies and the intelligence community that is relevant to determine whether to issue a visa or to determine the admissibility or deportability of an alien (also known as the “Chimera system”). […] In the development and implementation of the data system under this subsection, the President shall consult with the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and any such other agency as may be deemed appropriate.
events.attribution: Sec. 202(a)(2)–(3), enrolled text of H.R. 3525 (Pub. L. 107–173)

events.what: Entry suspended for 90 days, as immigrants and as visitors, for nationals of Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.
events.title: EO 13769 — entry suspension for seven countries
events.quote: […] pursuant to section 212(f) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1182(f), I hereby proclaim that the immigrant and nonimmigrant entry into the United States of aliens from countries referred to in section 217(a)(12) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1187(a)(12), would be detrimental to the interests of the United States, and I hereby suspend entry into the United States, as immigrants and nonimmigrants, of such persons for 90 days from the date of this order (excluding those foreign nationals traveling on diplomatic visas, North Atlantic Treaty Organization visas, C-2 visas for travel to the United Nations, and G-1, G-2, G-3, and G-4 visas).

events.what: A change in how the State Department counts its monthly visa figures. A change in the numbers, not in who came: nothing on the map is lit.
events.title: Visa Office changes the monthly reporting basis
events.src: “Monthly Nonimmigrant Visa Issuance Statistics”, note on the change of methodology · travel.state.gov
events.quote: The Visa Office has changed its methodology for calculating visa data beginning with the Fiscal Year (FY) 2019 annual Report of the Visa Office […] The new methodology more accurately reflects final outcomes from the visa application process during a specified reporting period. […] Therefore, beginning with FY 2020, individual monthly issuance reports should not be aggregated, as this will not provide an accurate issuance total for the fiscal year to date. Please note that the new methodology is only being applied to the monthly NIV issuance reports below, beginning with the October 2019 reports.
events.attribution: “Monthly Nonimmigrant Visa Issuance Statistics”, note on the change of methodology

events.what: The Census re-bases its estimates of how many people arrive and leave. It changes the US count, not the world.
events.title: 2020 census re-bases the population estimates
events.src: “New Population Estimates Show Historic Decline in Net International Migration”, on the Vintage 2025 methodology · census.gov
events.quote: Unlike previous vintages, we did not adjust the American Community Survey (ACS) data used in the non-U.S.-born immigration estimate for July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, because of its closeness to available administrative data. We analyzed a variety of data sources to improve our estimates of non-U.S.-born emigration. We used survey data from Mexico to update our estimates of non-U.S.-born emigration and net native migration. We updated our projections for the next estimates year (July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026) to reflect trends since January.
events.attribution: “New Population Estimates Show Historic Decline in Net International Migration”, on the Vintage 2025 methodology

events.what: Entry suspended for people who had recently been in China, Iran, the Schengen area, the UK or Ireland.
events.src: Proclamations 9984, 9992, 9993 and 9996 (Jan–Mar 2020). Map: visas by nationality, a stand-in for where people had been.
events.title: COVID-19 suspension of immigrant entry

events.what: Entry as immigrants suspended for anyone outside the US without an immigrant visa already in hand, from every country.
events.note: Dots are visas (temporary); the measure is green cards.
events.title: Proclamation 10014 — immigrant entry suspended
events.quote: The entry into the United States of aliens as immigrants is hereby suspended and limited subject to section 2 of this proclamation. […] (a) The suspension and limitation on entry pursuant to section 1 of this proclamation shall apply only to aliens who: (i) are outside the United States on the effective date of this proclamation; (ii) do not have an immigrant visa that is valid on the effective date of this proclamation;

events.what: The suspension extended to H-1B, H-2B, L and some J visas: skilled workers, seasonal workers, transferees and exchange visitors.
events.note: Lit: H-1B, exchange and other-work visas (the group that holds H-2B and L).
events.title: Proclamation 10052 — extended to H, L and J visas
events.quote: The entry into the United States of any alien seeking entry pursuant to any of the following nonimmigrant visas is hereby suspended and limited, subject to section 3 of this proclamation: (a) an H-1B or H-2B visa, and any alien accompanying or following to join such alien; (b) a J visa, to the extent the alien is participating in an intern, trainee, teacher, camp counselor, au pair, or summer work travel program, and any alien accompanying or following to join such alien; and (c) an L visa, and any alien accompanying or following to join such alien.

events.what: Proclamation 10014 revoked: it “does not advance the interests of the United States”.
events.note: Dots are visas (temporary); the measure is green cards.
events.title: Proclamation 10014 revoked
events.quote: The suspension of entry imposed in Proclamation 10014 of April 22, 2020 […] does not advance the interests of the United States. To the contrary, it harms the United States, including by preventing certain family members of United States citizens and lawful permanent residents from joining their families here. It also harms industries in the United States that utilize talent from around the world. And it harms individuals who were selected to receive the opportunity to apply for […] immigrant visas through the Fiscal Year 2020 Diversity Visa Lottery. […] Proclamation 10014, section 1 of Proclamation 10052, and section 1 of Proclamation 10131 are revoked.

events.what: Ukrainians displaced by Russia's war may apply to come on parole, for up to two years.
events.note: Parole is not a visa, so those who came on it do not appear here.
events.title: Uniting for Ukraine parole process
events.src: “Implementation of the Uniting for Ukraine Parole Process”, 87 FR 25040, Summary · dhs.gov
events.quote: This notice announces the implementation of a U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) parole process called Uniting for Ukraine. DHS will offer certain Ukrainian citizens and their immediate family members who were recently displaced by Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine, pass biometric and biographic vetting, have sufficient financial support in the United States, and meet other eligibility requirements, an opportunity to apply for and receive advance authorization to travel to the United States for the purpose of seeking a discretionary grant of parole for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit for up to two years.
events.attribution: “Implementation of the Uniting for Ukraine Parole Process”, 87 FR 25040, Summary

events.what: Title 42 expulsions end; a parole process opens for Cubans, Haitians and Nicaraguans, modelled on the one for Venezuelans.
events.note: Parole is not a visa, so those who came on it do not appear here.
events.title: Title 42 expulsions end
events.src: “DHS Continues to Prepare for End of Title 42” · state.gov
events.quote: DHS continues to prepare for the end of the Title 42 public health order, which is currently the subject of multiple court orders, and a return to processing all noncitizens under the Department's Title 8 immigration authorities. […] DHS is establishing new parole processes for Cubans, Haitians, and Nicaraguans, modeled on the successful processes for Venezuelans and Ukrainians, which combine safe, orderly, and lawful pathways to the United States, including authorization to work, with significant consequences for those who fail to use those pathways.
events.attribution: “DHS Continues to Prepare for End of Title 42”

events.what: New H-1B workers may enter only if a $100,000 payment comes with the petition.
events.title: Proclamation — $100,000 H-1B entry payment
events.src: Proclamation of 19 September 2025, “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers”, Sec. 1(a) · uscis.gov
events.note: It took effect on 21 September 2025, nine days before FY2025 ended: its effect is not in these numbers yet.
events.quote: Pursuant to sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), […] the entry into the United States of aliens as nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA, […] is restricted, except for those aliens whose petitions are accompanied or supplemented by a payment of $100,000—subject to the exceptions set forth in subsection (c) of this section. This restriction shall expire, absent extension, 12 months after the effective date of this proclamation, which shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on September 21, 2025.
events.attribution: Proclamation of 19 September 2025, “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers”, Sec. 1(a)
